pharm: A class of high-potassium (and additive-containing) solutions delivered into the coronary circulation during cardiac surgery to induce rapid diastolic cardiac arrest and protect the myocardium during aortic cross-clamping.
quick: Variable; e.g., del Nido ~20 mL/kg single dose into coronary circulation
Used as needed for maternal cardiac surgery
Account for electrolyte load (K+) in renal impairment
Cardiac arrest/recovery, serum K+, ECG, acid-base
summary: Cardioplegia refers to a group of solutions, not a single FDA-approved drug, used during cardiac surgery to stop the heart in diastole and protect the myocardium during ischemic arrest on cardiopulmonary bypass. Formulations include crystalloid and blood-based, warm or cold, and antegrade or retrograde delivery; common protocols are del Nido and St. Thomas (cold high-potassium) solutions. The core arresting agent is potassium chloride; additives (magnesium, lidocaine, mannitol, bicarbonate) prolong arrest and protect cells.
indications: Induction and maintenance of diastolic cardiac arrest during open-heart/cardiac surgery on cardiopulmonary bypass
Myocardial protection during aortic cross-clamping (CABG, valve, congenital, aortic surgery)
Preservation of donor hearts and protection during other procedures requiring a still, protected myocardium

dosage.t: Single dose; redose typically after ~60-90 min of cross-clamp
dosage.n: 4:1 crystalloid-to-blood ratio; K+ ~24-26 mEq/L delivered, with lidocaine, magnesium, mannitol, bicarbonate
Extracellular high-K+ solution (sodium, potassium, chloride, magnesium, bicarbonate)
Volumes and composition adjusted to age/weight by the surgical team

admin: Administered by the surgical/perfusion team into the coronary circulation (antegrade via aortic root/coronary ostia or retrograde via the coronary sinus)
Delivered cold or warm and as crystalloid or blood-mixed per the chosen protocol (e.g., del Nido 4:1 crystalloid:blood)
Induce arrest, then redose intermittently or use single-dose technique depending on solution and cross-clamp time
Monitor for complete diastolic arrest and electrical silence on ECG
Wash out/flush before reperfusion; manage potassium and acid-base on reperfusion
moa: Potassium chloride raises extracellular potassium, depolarizing the myocyte membrane and arresting the heart in diastole, which markedly lowers myocardial oxygen demand and preserves intracellular ATP during ischemia. Additives extend protection: lidocaine blocks sodium channels (limiting sodium/calcium loading), magnesium stabilizes membranes and antagonizes calcium, mannitol provides osmotic/free-radical protection, and bicarbonate buffers ischemic acidosis. Cooling further reduces metabolic demand.

absolute: Use outside the intraoperative cardiac-surgery setting
Direct intravenous (systemic) administration as a routine drug (concentrated potassium is cardiotoxic systemically)
monitor: ECG and myocardial recovery on reperfusion

preg: Used as clinically required for maternal cardiac surgery; managed by the surgical and obstetric team with attention to maternal-fetal perfusion.
lact: Not applicable - single intraoperative use; resume breastfeeding per perioperative guidance.
renal: Account for the potassium load; in renal impairment monitor serum potassium closely during and after bypass and manage hyperkalemia on reperfusion.

major: Systemic effects of delivered potassium (hyperkalemia) on reperfusion - monitor and treat
Additive cardiac effects with antiarrhythmics in the perioperative period
moderate: Calcium administration may antagonize the arresting effect / precipitate reperfusion injury if mistimed
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor intraoperative electrolytes (potassium), arterial blood gases, and ECG.

serious: Difficulty weaning from bypass / post-cardiotomy ventricular dysfunction
Reperfusion arrhythmias (e.g., ventricular fibrillation requiring defibrillation)
Inadequate myocardial protection leading to ischemic injury
emergency: Failure of the heart to resume effective contraction (myocardial stunning/failure)

monitoring: Completeness and maintenance of diastolic arrest (ECG silence)
Arterial blood gases and acid-base balance
Cardiac rhythm and contractility on reperfusion/weaning from bypass
counsel: This is an intraoperative solution given by your surgical and perfusion team to stop and protect your heart during surgery - not a take-home medicine
Your heart is intentionally stopped during part of the operation and restarted afterward
Temporary heart-rhythm changes and electrolyte shifts can occur as the heart restarts and are managed by the team
Ask your surgeon about the specific myocardial-protection strategy used in your operation
pk: Diastolic arrest within seconds to a minute of coronary delivery
Single-dose (e.g., del Nido) up to ~60-90 min; St. Thomas redosed every ~20-30 min
Refrigerate cold solutions per protocol; mix with blood and cool at point of use
pearls: NOTE: Cardioplegia is a class/group of solutions, not a single FDA-approved drug; composition and delivery vary by institution and protocol
Potassium chloride is the core arresting agent (depolarized diastolic arrest); additives prolong and refine protection
del Nido (single-dose, 4:1 crystalloid:blood, with lidocaine + magnesium) vs. St. Thomas (intermittent, repeated every 20-30 min) are the two most common adult protocols
del Nido uses lower potassium but lasts longer because of magnesium and lidocaine
Must never be given as a routine systemic IV drug - concentrated potassium is cardiotoxic
missed: Not applicable - administered intraoperatively by the perfusion team; redosing is dictated by cross-clamp time and the chosen solution protocol, not patient self-administration.
overdose: Excess delivery raises systemic potassium and can cause hyperkalemia, refractory arrest, and reperfusion arrhythmias. Management: stop delivery, wash out cardioplegia, correct hyperkalemia (calcium, insulin-glucose, bicarbonate, diuresis/dialysis as needed), support the myocardium, and treat arrhythmias.
